THE INTEREST OF PSYCHOANALYSIS IN THE WORK AND LIVES of great artists, as in Freud's classic study of Leonardo (1910) or his reflections on the Moses of Michelangelo (1924), has multiple purposes. From the point of view of psychoanalysis, it provides the opportunity for exploration of patterns of meaningful involvement in the artist's life and experience that come to bear in his artistic efforts and lend support from an extraclinical frame of reference for putative psychoanalytic hypotheses, whether developmental or pathological. From the artistic perspective, it lends another dimension to the understanding of the meaning of the artist's work and offers hopefully a deeper understanding of the roots of artistic creativity. I propose in this essay to explore a specific theme in the life and work of Vincent van Gogh that played itself out as a persistent and recurrent leitmotif from the very beginning of his life, had powerful determining influence on his life experience and his interpersonal relationships, and provided a powerful current in the dynamic processes underlying his immense artistic creativity. The theme I have in mind is that of the double.

The theme of the double has played a role in the unconscious fantasy of many creative individuals. It has played a prominent part in the creative lives of writers and artists through the ages (Rank, 1914), (1971) ; (Grotstein, 1983) ; (Rogers, 1970). The theme was enunciated by Freud (1919) in his description of the double as arising from the unconscious, another self that is both hostile and sympathetic. But, as Eder (1978) notes, "Doubles are of two kinds. Either the double is an exact replica, mirror image, or identical twin … or the double is one's other self, a self irrupting from the unconscious, that is antithetical yet complementary to one's conscious self" (p. 579). Daniel Gensler  

PSYCHOANALYTICALLY ORIENTED CHILD THERAPISTS usually value dreams. As a child learns that the therapist values dreams, the child may report them more often, out of the pleasure of pleasing the analyst and of doing something together with the analyst. There may or may not be the additional pleasure of making connections between the dreams and something significant in the child's life. On the other hand, if the child sees that dreams refer to anxious wishes or fears, the child may ward off the therapist's interest so as not to have to face the anxiety. The child may resent the therapist's interest, ignore it, refuse to cooperate and withhold the dream. Whether the child welcomes or resists the therapist's interest in dreams, an area of interest is being identified which was never so clearly valued before.

The child may take the therapist's interest in other ways as well. The child may simply feel encouraged to look further at the dream. After all, in offering a nonjudgmental, empathic inquiry into dream material, the therapist is a new object for the child, who has never before considered such material so carefully. Alternately, the child may take the therapist's interest in dreams as a chance to tease or provoke the therapist; to test the genuineness of the therapist's interest; or to devalue the therapist's interest.

MY FIRST REACTION to being asked to discuss children's dreams was the recognition that in fact I did not know much about children's dreams and I wondered if it might be better if someone else had been asked. That I did not know much about children's dreams struck me as a little strange as I consider myself skilled in working with children. I rely heavily on dreams with adults, but, unless the child brings one up, I rarely discuss them. When I examined why I treat them this way I realized that I do not discuss children's dreams because I find for the most part that they are much too direct, and, outside of some broad generalizations, I often do not wish for the child to know much about his unconscious dynamics. The child is in the process of building defenses and it is not a good idea to reveal them before they are in place. I shall explain more about this later in my paper.

In searching some of the literature I became a little upset in noting that in some ways I am re-inventing the wheel and that some of my observations about children's dreams have been made before. However, I am critical about ways in which other analysts have worked with children's dreams which I will note, but of course as I reveal my own thoughts I suspect that some of you might be critical of my approach. "People in glass houses shouldn't etc., " or as the Nepalese more graphically word it, "Do not look for lice on your neighbor's head when there is a water buffalo sitting on your own head."

There is a good summary of the psychoanalytic application of children's dreams by Ablon and Mack (1980).

FREUD WROTE IN 1910 to his Hungarian colleague Sandor Ferenczi about a new case he had started. In the first session the new patient "confessed to me the following transferences: Jewish swindler, he would like to use me from behind and shit on my head" (Gay, 1988, p. 287). A lively beginning to the case that produced the Wolf-Man dream, the second most famous dream in the psychoanalytic literature after the Irma dream.

Sergei Pankejeff, the Wolf-Man, came to Freud in February of 1910 and the treatment continued until July 1914. He had been unsuccessfully treated by two of Freud's enemies, Theodor Ziehen and Emil Kraepelin. The treatment began in a sanitarium and was later transferred to Freud's private practice in his home at Bergasse 19. The patient was a severely disturbed young man of 23, the only son of an extremely wealthy aristocratic Russian family. His health had deteriorated at age 18 after a gonorrhea infection and he became incapacitated and had to be cared for by others. His father had been diagnosed as manic-depressive and his mother was both physically ill and hypochondriacal. His sister and only sibling, two years older, a very brilliant young woman to whom he was very attached, had treated him sadistically in childhood, became emotionally disturbed in adolescence, and committed suicide at age 21. He grew up on a large estate near Odessa, lonely and emotionally abandoned by his parents who often travelled, leaving him in the hands of a governess.

IN THIS PAPER, I BRING SOME INSIGHTS from the field of anthropology to bear on the point of view expressed by Fromm in Ch. III. (1) Fromm saw existential anxiety over the certainty of death as a fundamental and primary force in all human cultures. (2) To explore this existential anxiety as the organizing principle for cultures, I will discuss three preliterate cultures, from very different ecological settings and backgrounds. (3) In this analysis it becomes apparant that existential death anxiety derives more from the beliefs and values of a secular Western culture. The three world views of the Dani, Ojibwa and Yanomamo are seen as systems for organizing blame or guilt. This corresponds to a group form of Sullivan's notion of parataxis. (4) The enduring value of Fromm's work is in the issues he raised and the questions he asked about the human situation.

To the Editor:

READING "OUT OF OUR MINDS, " (Volume 29:453–478) I was particularly moved by the discussion of relevance: the patient's need to feel that the therapist (and everybody else) will treat him/her as someone who counts, someone who really matters.

As an artist—someone who works in solitude and must get used to very little encouragement from the outside world—I also find the issue of relevance puzzling. Even the most successful painter, sculptor, writer, or composer spends most of his days alone in a room, where another human being rarely looks over his shoulder and says "How wonderful!" Artists go for years between exhibitions. Writers go for years between books. Composers write music that may never be performed. How can we live this way?

When the outside world gives us so little reason to believe that we're relevant, where do we find the elusive feeling that we matter at all? The truth, of course, is that most would-be artists, writers, and composers give up and disappear soon after they leave school. But some of us do keep going all our lives despite the fact that so few people seem to care. Do the survivors know something that other people may not know? What makes us survivors? LANGS'S PAPER IS ABOUT the what not the how. It's a nice distillation, a précis of his concepts of empowered psychotherapy, which uses what he calls self-processing. It includes a hypothesis that the human mind consists of two parallel processing systems, each with different perceptual adaptive repertoires and responses to anxiety. They're two very different realms of experience and adaptation. The first system itself has two parts, its own conscious and unconscious mechanisms. They have to do with coping with realistic dangers and gratifying needs and necessities such as food, shelter and companionship, sort of like Sullivan's self-system involving satisfactions and security. While messages from this somewhat superficial unconscious system tend to be encoded, they are readily translatable and understood. Langs gives the example of the lateness of a doctor encoded as the lateness of a teacher.

For the more serious and profound anxieties Langs postulates another "deeper" unconscious system. (Are we back with Freud's topology?) This one proves to be remarkably sensitive to the rules, frames and boundaries in life's situations, and, by extension, in psychotherapy (a touch of anthropomorphism?). Langs states that boundary issues are of primary significance because they are crucial to the survival of the living organism, and therefore have critical functions and meanings. True, but how does the psychoanalyst tend to think of boundaries? Does respect for a boundary refer to insularity, to maintaining the status quo, or is a reliable boundary a metaphor for processes of union and differentiatedness?

THE PSYCHOANALYST MEETS A very real human struggle in each clinical hour. Unfortunately, the romanticism of psychoanalytic commentary mystifies the difficulty of this struggle by imposing upon it a loftiness of mythic proportion. THIS HARVEST OF PAPERS was reaped in response to an invitation extended to several analysts of varied backgrounds. Each of them was urged to comment freely on Chapter III of Erich Fromm's (1947) Man for Himself, an excerpt from which (pp. 44–49) is included here. This particular statement by Fromm is selected for special attention as a relatively early yet full expression of themes that endured in his writings until his death in 1980. My first encounter with Man for Himself still is vivid in memory for its direct challenge to the credo of scientific neutrality into which my generation of psychoanalysts and social scientists had been educated.

The issues he posed so long ago continue to confront analysts each day, pervasively woven into their exchanges with patients. Therefore it is worthwhile to test out how well his position has weathered the intervening years. To judge by this small but thoughtful group of writers, at least one part of Fromm's thesis is now well established. It is the impossibility of moral neutrality in the consulting room. But as an alternative to neutrality, his advocacy of a humanistic ethic, that provides a universal guide to both a sane society and individual mental health, has aroused skepticism. From a social constructivist perspective, it has a curiously ethnocentric flavor.

But to say more is to encroach upon the observations made by the individual discussants who comprise this symposium.

MEISTER ECKHART WHOM ERICH FROMM CHOSE to provide an epigraph for Chapter III of his book Man for Himself, was a Dominican monk from Thuringia, who lived from about 1260 to about 1329. He studied in Paris, among other places, was strongly influenced by the philosophy of Thomas Aquinas, and has been principally known for his sermons in German and Latin, in which a profoundly mystical version of Christianity appears. He presided after 1307 over the Dominican province that extended from the Netherlands to Prague, governing fifty monasteries of friars and nine houses of nuns. His writings are charged with the intense spirituality of his period, during which mystical teachers and preachers of the church abounded. Many of the hierarchy were disturbed by seemingly pantheistic implications latent in his sermons, certain passages of which were officially condemned. That he was ever anything but an orthodox Christian and a devoted priest and pastor to his immense flock was never claimed, nor is it evident from his writings. The passage Fromm quotes is characteristic of Eckhart's challenging expression, but he cannot be included among those who are convinced that man must "acknowledge his fundamental aloneness and solitude in a universe indifferent to his fate, [and] recognize that there is no power transcending him." Quite the contrary, Eckhart's constant appeal is that we recognize God-within-us, the God of the Bible and of Catholic Christian doctrine. He is no agnostic humanist.

The point of these references is not academic or historical. Agnostic or atheist humanism has been taken for granted as the spiritual position of the heirs of the Enlightenment, including us of the Freudian tradition. Humanistic reflections on religion and ethics normally depart from a position, supposed to be demonstrable if not self-evident, of interpreting religious beliefs as comforting or otherwise functional illusions, assembled in rival ideologies all of which make untenable claims to truth. My intention is to examine Fromm's remarks in this chapter from another point of view. Fromm's humanism is not here in question.

There is no innate "drive for progress" in man; it is the contradiction in his existence that makes him proceed on the way he set out. Having lost paradise, the unity with nature, he has become the eternal wanderer (Odysseus, Oedipus, Abraham, Faust); he is impelled to go forward and with everlasting effect to make the unknown known by filling in with answers the blank spaces of his knowledge. Fromm points out that our existence is rooted in contradictions, the awareness of which is so painful and difficult to sustain, that we are driven to create various illusions to shore up our anxieties and hold our hopes. Also, living in a certain historical era and system, we are limited by its institutions and values. Fromm reminds us that while existential dichotomies are not alterable, historical ones can be changed, but not necessarily during our lifetime. If such historical change occurs, we do feel a profound sense of renewal and limitless hope, as we did when the totalitarian regimes collapsed in Eastern Europe and Russia. Notes on Psychoanalytic Supervision

To the Editor:

QUESTIONS ABOUT SUPERVISION still abound. Despite the impressive burgeoning of literature about it during the past decade, many critical issues about the contemporary ordering of supervision are still unanswered. And these are, in my view, not separate but derivative from central issues about psychoanalytic therapy itself, also still unanswered. They concern how best to study the convergences of transference and countertransference in the field of therapy in which they are always live and often interlock, also rarely planned and often unanticipated; and then, of course, how best to study them in a field of supervision once removed from the shared experience in which they first appear.

In fact, the manner in which these two fields of inquiry relate to one another—whether they are detached or derivative, divergent or descendant one from the other—is also a matter of considerable disagreement. The reason for it is not hard to fathom. The three individuals who interact in these two fields—supervisor and therapist, therapist and patient—never truly control the variable conditions and contents of their respective interactions. The relationship of supervisor and therapist does not, in any obvious sense, replicate the relationship of therapist and patient. Nor should it be expected to.

Readers are invited to send in brief commentaries or critical evaluations of issues raised in this Journal or in the psychoanalytic field in general. These communications should be no more than eight pages, and should be addressed to the Editor.

THIS BOOK IS FOR STUDENTS of psychoanalysis who, as graduate students, were trained primarily in the logic and methods of established scientific inquiry. It's part of a long-standing effort to apply rules of measurement to frequency of occurrence, developed in the laboratory sciences, to recurrent elements of psychoanalytic interaction precisely because the quantitative analysis of probabilistic inference has proved so fruitful in other scientific fields of investigation. It holds interest for researchers who work from the known to the unknown, not for therapists who are caught up in the sweat, tears, and messiness of daily practice with wide varieties of patients, and whose narrative constructions of human pain and suffering fail to encompass their patients's psychic reality with adequate sense and meaning. Within the limited space here, I present some reasons for these reactions.

Recall that Freud, the creator of Spence's rhetorical voice, never became a premier therapist. He even gave up, eventually, on the possible future of psychoanalysis as therapy. He never knew what it's like to undergo the experience himself: he neither went into personal therapy nor gave patients access to his countertransference. To his lasting credit, however, he always extolled Ferenczi, whose clinical work Spence ignores, as the therapist par excellence of that first generation: he also regarded Breuer, whose innovative work Spence doesn't mention, as having made the cornerstone discovery of psychoanalysis—that is, the theory of unconscious psychic experience.

When we tell the patient to say everything which comes to mind, the message is that sins of commission are preferable to sins of omission. In other words, withholding from the analyst is worse than letting it all hang out. Sins of omission on the patient's part are called by the pejorative label of resistance. These rules are a holdover from the time when it was believed that it was possible and preferable to conceal the analyst's personality behind neutrality and abstinence, but that the patient should divulge everything which came to mind. Well, now we recognize that the analyst cannot hide his or her personality and that patients do not always say everything. When words fail them for whatever reason, patients resort to acting out in the transference, communicating nonverbally through projective identification, etc. By the same token, since neutrality is impossible, analysts also, none too rarely, find themselves acting out their countertransferences, communicating nonverbally through what has been called projective counteridentification (Grindberg, 1983), etc.

What has been lost especially, in the attempt for the analyst to be circumspect with the patient, is the role that the analyst's affective reactions have in the interplay, both conscious and unconscious, between patient and analyst. Although we as analysts are in an exciting period of theoretical, research and technical growth, in terms of our understanding of the relationship between patient and analyst, there still is room to pay more attention to the omnipresent affective aspects of the therapeutic process. Borrowing a phrase from Joyce McDougall, this paper is a plea for a measure of affectivity. I will address what I see as a need for an increased awareness on our parts as analysts of the interplay of affect between the two participants. Particularly, I would like to focus on the role played by the patient's success in getting the analyst to feel what it is they are nonverbally and unconsciously transmitting to us—that is, projective identification.

HISTORICALLY, THE CONCEPT OF DISSOCIATION is usually distinguished from that of repression based upon earlier vs. later developmental themes and/or severity of anxiety. Dissociation has traditionally been associated with traumatic or profound anxiety occurring either in pre-verbal times or, if later, potentially of annihilating proportion. Anxiety-laden experience cannot be processed either verbally or emotionally, since the psyche is too undeveloped or fragile to even assimilate the experience, or the assault on the psyche is too profound. Repression, in contrast, is usually thought to occur either when anxiety-laden events can be put into words, the psyche is strong enough to handle them or the experience is anxiety-producing but not annihilation-producing. Dissociation then has traditionally been discussed as reflecting earlier and/or more severe psychological disruption, essentially inaccessible to subsequent awareness. Davies and Frawley (1992) have referred to the vertical split of dissociation in contrast with the horizontal split of repression.

The Concept of Structure

THE CONCEPT OF STRUCTURE IS INVOKED in most references to psychological processes that are stable over time. The idea of structure grows from the assumption that experience and behavior are appearances or manifestations of underlying templates or foundations, which themselves may never be observable. In the psychological and psychoanalytic literature of the twentieth century, the assumption of structure is nearly ubiquitous. Apart from neurophysiology, it is the primary way we have had to grasp and represent in theoretical terms how and why conduct and experience manifest regularities.

Structural concepts are backbones in all fields defined by the study of the human condition. Cognitive psychology, for example, is devoted to the identification of the regularities in our processing of information. Advances are therefore measured in terms of structural theories that can account for old data and predict new ones. Some of these mechanisms are assumed to be direct manifestations of neurophysiology. Others, though, are combinations of neurophysiology with representations of past experience, encoded and transformed into channels for new experience. A newly proposed cognitive mechanism, for example, might allow the established theories to stretch around otherwise anomalous phenomena of perception, thought, or memory.

IN VIEW OF THE FACT THAT PATIENTS have been talking about their dreams and analysts writing about them for the best part of a century, it is striking that very few analysts have wished to write about their patients' dreams of them. The Chicago Psychoanalytic Index, for example, documents that analysts have been prolifically interested in their patients' dreams about beer, cakes, rings and razors but over the past fifty years there are perhaps no more than a dozen papers about dreams of the analyst, and a number of those mention the significance of such dreams only peripherally. Analysts on the whole are not noted for their reluctance to come forward with ideas about the meaning of clinical data, so the apparent dearth of interest in our patients' dreams of us is worthy of note. Freud (1923) in a paper concerned with the practical implications of working with dreams pointed out that the manifest content of patients' dreams is necessarily influenced by occurrences in the analysis itself, and that it is no disgrace when this happens. Why, therefore, have dreams of the analyst proved a relatively uninviting area for comment and exploration? It is tempting to speculate and since, as Oscar Wilde said, "The only way to get rid of a temptation is to yield to it, " allow me briefly to speculate.

Freudian drive theory requires that dreams be seen as compromise formations, along with jokes, symptoms and parapraxes. As a result of the dream work, unacceptable instinctual impulses are able to elude the dream censor and find limited discharge or expression. This model also requires that each dream be seen as made up of latent content, the hidden instinctual depths, and manifest content, the story the dreamer remembers and tells to us. Russell Meares M.D.

Russell Meares

Russell Meares, M.D.
Department of Psychiatry University of Sydney Westmead Hospital
Westmead, New South Wales 2145
Australia

Russell Meares  

A 35 YEAR OLD MAN Mr A, develops an extraordinary series of routines which guard against the possibility of being observed from the street while he undresses in his bedroom. This is the first symptom of an obsessive-compulsive disorder. He resembles those in Janet's classic series whose sense of exposure was such that they needed to be totally alone when undressing (Pitman, 1984, p. 310). Mr A exhibits what might be called a pathology of privacy. This is the main point of this paper, the thesis of which is that an important determinant of obsessive-compulsive disorder is a threatened or deficient conception of an inner life. This idea links to Sullivan's remarks about the hypocrisy which characterises the early family life of those with obsessive-compulsive disorder. Such a background, it will be argued, is likely to impede the mature attainment of the concept of self-boundary. The main thesis leads to a therapeutic approach to obsessive-compulsive disorder which focuses on a central feature of the illness, which Freud identified and called "the omnipotence of thoughts" (Freud, 1913).

Freud wrote fourteen papers on obsessive-compulsive disorder. He found it "unquestionably the most interesting and repaying subject of analytic research." He also considered that "as a problem it has not yet been mastered" (Freud, 1926). His remark still applies. The illness remains a mystery. Since Freud's time, psychoanalytic interest in obsessive-compulsive disorder has waned. No systematic examination of the subject has been made since the 1965 Congress of the International Psychoanalytical Association as Esman notes (Esman, 1988).

THERE IS A GREAT DEAL OF commonality between the Interpersonal and Jungian approaches to dream interpretation, which has not previously been fully recognized or explored. There are striking similarities in the use of 'manifest content, ' and in the conceptualization of the types of mental operations that occur in sleep. These, and other similarities, will be discussed below. In fact, the evolution of the Interpersonal approach to dreams and dream interpretation, as developed by Sullivan (1953) and Fromm (1951), owes a considerable and largely unacknowledged debt to Jung (1933). Besides the existing areas of overlap, there are additional aspects of the Jungian approach that have not yet been considered by Interpersonalists, which could help to expand and refine the Interpersonal approach.

Sullivan's approach to dreams is characterized by a certain ambivalence (Sullivan, 1953). Dreams are considered to contain very important information about the dreamer, but the use of dream interpretation in treatment is cautioned against. Sullivan (1953) offers several examples of dream interpretation, but avoids spelling out specific principles for dream interpretation.

Sullivan viewed sleep as a time when the self system is temporarily relaxed, because threats to self-esteem are at a distance (Sullivan, 1953). Thought processes are relatively less interfered with by anxiety. Motivational tendencies and self/other personifications that are normally dissociated can be safely expressed. In this way sleep and dreams act as a safety valve for the personality. PSYCHOANALYSIS IS HAUNTED BY a peculiar dilemma. For all of the immense effort which has been invested in metapsychological theories, and for all the subsequent, and often acrimonious disputations about their comparative values; there remains considerable doubt about the relevance of those theories to the practice of psychoanalytic psychotherapy. Anna Freud, in 1969 said, "[Theory] … has become the bugbear of the clinically oriented analyst who feels wholly divorced from it"; a skepticism still shared by many practitioners of the craft, who genuflect in the direction of their institutional canons—and then do whatever they think works (A. Freud, 1969, p. 386). Astute clinicians have always understood that they were, in Masud Khan's felicitous phrase, "the servants of the patient's process".1 That is, therapy proceeded by our tapping into, and melding with, a mysterious flow, a conflux, which defies the linear explanations provided by metapsychologies which explain everything and understand nothing. The Sufi's were wont to say, somewhat sarcastically, "No problem is too difficult for a theoretician". If this were really so, then any polished theoretician would be ipso facto an accomplished clinician; and that is clearly not the case. Talking knowledgeably about something is not at all the same as doing it.

COMMUNICATION BETWEEN PARENT AND CHILD and the construction of reality as a mutually engaging process are central issues in psychoanalytic theories of development. Sullivan (1953) commenting on the nearly magical quality of verbal language to evoke or inhibit the kind of empathic responsiveness from caregivers that facilitates psychological growth, stated, "The infant's success in the field of language behavior carries a very high premium so far as favorable, tender response of the significant elder figures is concerned."

Language allows the social values of one generation to be passed onto the next. It is through verbal interaction that children begin to distinguish fantasy from reality and arrive at some sense of themselves and others, their worth, and the environment in which they live. Through language the child and parents construct a world where objects have names, sensory experiences are shared, logical connections made. With shared language, the process of consensual validation between parent and child begins to occur (Sullivan, 1953). Parents and child create a framework for their relationship, and then can talk about that shared reality.

Vygotsky's work (1934) on the role of language and social interaction in the development of concept formation addresses the same issue. His concept of the "Zone of Proximal Development" is "an account of how the more competent assist the young and the less competent to reach that higher ground, ground from which to reflect more abstractly about the nature of things" (Bruner, 1986 p. 73).

Introduction

PROJECTIVE IDENTIFICATION IS A CONCEPT that has undergone a sea-change in its purported meaning. First described by Tausk (1919) as the mechanism behind the influencing machine, it was alluded to in other terms by Freud in his papers, "On Narcissism" (1914), and "Group Psychology and the Analysis of the Ego" (1921). It was Klein who formally defined the concept after finding so much evidence for the presence of this mechanism in primitive mental life and in the play therapy of children. She at first was aware of it as projection, per se, a well known mechanism from the earliest days of psychoanalysis and associated it with the infant's desire to rid itself of its aggressive impulses (Klein, 1921). In 1946, however, Klein elevated projection, an instinctual mode, to projective identification, an object-relations (and especially a part -object relations) mode of relating. Since then there have been debates between Kleinians and non-Kleinians, particularly Americans, over whether there is a distinction between projection and projective identification. Non-Kleinians, who, in general, are unfamiliar and/or untrained in primitive part-object relations are usually unable to appreciate the Kleinian conception that there can be no projection without the translocation of the projecting subject's identification.

Erich Fromm

Erich Fromm

Erich Fromm  

MAN CAN REACT TO HISTORICAL contradictions by annulling them through his own action; but he cannot annual existential dichotomies, although he can react to them in different ways. He can appease his mind by soothing and harmonizing ideologies. He can try to escape from his inner restlessness by ceaseless activity in pleasure or business. He can try to abrogate his freedom and to turn himself into an instrument of powers outside himself, submerging his self in them. But he remains dissatisfied, anxious, and restless. There is only one solution to his problem: to face the truth, to acknowledge his fundamental aloneness and solitude in a universe indifferent to his fate, to recognize that there is no power transcending him which can solve his problem for him. Man must accept the responsibility for himself and the fact that only by using his own powers can he give meaning to his life. But meaning does not imply certainty; indeed, the quest for certainty blocks the search for meaning. Uncertainty is the very condition to impel man to unfold his powers. If he faces the truth without panic he will recognize that there is no meaning to life except the meaning man gives his life by the unfolding of his powers, by living productively ; and that only constant vigilance, activity, and effort can keep us from failing in the one task that matters—the full development of our powers within the limitations set by the laws of our existence. Man will never cease to be perplexed, to wonder, and to raise new questions. Only if he recognizes the human situation, the dichotomies inherent in his existence and his capacity to unfold his powers, will he be able to succeed in his task: to be himself and for himself and to achieve happiness by the full realization of those faculties which are peculiarly his—of reason, love, and productive work.

About Time

Harold Boris

Harold Boris

Harold N. Boris
632-34 Lewis Wharf
Boston, Massachusetts 02110-3924

Harold Boris  

What we call the beginning is often the end And to make an end is to make a beginning
—T. S. Eliot1

WHAT MAKES EXPERIENCE ENDURABLE or otherwise has at least something to do with knowing that there will be a time to it. Pleasure or unpleasure alike are qualified by the time they take. Can there be any pleasure so great as to survive its being ceaseless and endless? Is there any ordinary pain that cannot be endured if one knows that there will be an end to it?

To any experience, time is therefore a party. It accompanies experience dressed variously as ever and never; no longer and not yet; as beginning, ongoing, and ending; as soon or now or later; as quick or slow; as again and again or as never again. It is by no means clear how the sense of time evolves, only that to an extent it does.2 As analysts, we are certainly occupied with it: minutes per session, times per week, punctuality and tardiness, duration of the analysis, timing of interpretations, and much more. In a sense this occupation reflects the suspicion that our patients are insufficiently attuned to time—that the timelessness of the unconscious, and more specifically of the primary process that Freud dealt with at the start of his psychoanalytic formulations and of the analysis interminable that occupied him at the end, remain monitory touchstones for us. Indeed throughout Freud's work weaves the sinuous issue of time. It is in the genetic formulations, the idea of phase-development, the concept of regression, at the heart of the idea of transference, in the repetition compulsion, the death instinct, and even in the idea of Nirvana. Arendt (1971) described the experience of dialogue in individual thought, and she noted how the thinker experiences solitude but not loneliness; in effect, the thinker keeps herself company. I think Arendt's phrase, the "two-in-one, " can help us focus on two facts: that a single person can experience himself as a social group, and also, conversely, that a group of two or more people can experience itself as a single unit, although it is often difficult to find the words to describe such experiences. And so I prefer to think not in terms of the dichotomy, projective identification or countertransference, but instead to study the "two-in-one" of projective identification and countertransference.

I think that our natural human tendency to think in terms of dichotomies, which the neurobiologist Gerald Edelman (1987) thinks is wired into our brains, causes a lot of mischief in dealing with projective identification and countertransference. Any premature or excessive concern with the question of who is doing what to whom is not part of the analytic attitude, as I think of it. As analysts, we develop the ability to leave the questions of blame and attribution aside. Patients need the room to present psychological issues, often dissociated from their awareness, into the analytic field, without being hindered by premature explanation, closure, and attribution.

It is a fundamental principal of interpersonal psychoanalysis that dissociated tendencies often underlie psychopathology. Sullivan (1940) wrote in the Conceptions of Modern Psychiatry [p. 47]: "We may say, however, as a generality, that healthy development of personality is inversely proportionate to the amount and the number of tendencies which have come to exist in dissociation." In clinical psychoanalysis, projective identification allows a patient to look at his own dissociated personality tendencies as the properties of another person and to allow the drama of psychic conflict to be played out interpersonally, with the analyst as co-participant. The analyst can have very strange experiences in this situation, often feeling as if he is possessed by personality traits, thoughts, or emotions, the source of which he cannot at first identify. When faced with such a puzzling situation, the task of the analyst is not to decide whether he is experiencing projective identification or countertransference.

We are accustomed to attend with loving relish to almost every detail of a person's presentation, from the broad strokes of his or her lifestyle and interpersonal behavior, to the minutiae of his or her speech patterns, nuances of tone and eye movement, details of dress, and preferences for everything. THE TREATMENT OF PARTICULARLY vulnerable patients has highlighted the importance of non-interpretive aspects of psychoanalysis. Non-interpretive work refers to those dimensions of psychoanalytic process which involve an elaboration of the patient's experience of the analyst as a subjective or an objective object rather than as an agent of enhanced self understanding (Winnicott, 1971). Here, the analyst (temporarily) suspends attempts to acquire a fuller apprehension of internal process in order to address the patient's need for a particular emotional experience with the analytic object.

An especially intriguing and difficult dimension of non-interpretive work is described by Winnicott's (1971) concept of object usage. Winnicott used this notion to define a developmental achievement that involves the acquisition of a secure awareness of the object's autonomous existence, of the patient's capacity for loving and hating without threatening the object's survival.

In the sequence one can say that first there is object- relating, then in the end there is object-use; in between, however, is the most difficult thing, perhaps, in human development; or the most irksome of all the early failures that come for mending. This thing that there is in between relating and use is the subject's placing of the object outside the area of the subject's omnipotent control; that is, the subject's perception of the object as an external phenomenon, not as a projection … after 'subject relates to object' comes 'subject destroys object' (as it becomes external); and then may come 'object survives destruction by the subject' … From now on the subject says: 'Hullo object!' 'I destroyed you.' 'I love you.' 'You have value for me because of your survival of my destruction of you' (Winnicott, 1971, pp. 89–90).

It is therefore necessary to provide the conditions that will enhance the analysand's potential for engaging in the analytic work. THE MAJOR PURPOSE IN OUR PAPER IS to present a new concept about primary process functioning we have called primary process meaning analysis. By primary process meaning analysis we refer to a process in which the primary process system unconsciously organizes, evaluates, represents, and communicates the meanings of an individual's interactions with the external world. What have been labeled primary process derivatives are actually, in our opinion, the end-products of a process we call meaning analysis, in which individuals unconsciously represent the meanings they ascribe to their interactions with the environment and especially other persons (Dorpat & Miller, 1992).

Primary process derivatives include imagery, figures of speech (especially metaphors), nonverbal communications, affects, intuition, and some narratives. The theory advanced here about primary process meaning analysis differs from the traditional theory inasmuch as we do not believe that these derivatives are formed from unconscious fantasies.

In contrast to the traditional theory which conceptualizes the primary process as isolated from interactions with the outside world, our theory conceptualizes the primary process as having direct contact with the external world. In our previous publications we showed that the primary process system is immediately and directly involved with an individual's interactions with others (Dorpat, 1991) ; (Dorpat & Miller, 1992). This system unconsciously organizes and, thereby, attributes a meaning to such interactions in addition to also unconsciously representing and communicating the meanings ascribed to these interactions to others. IN THE PRECEEDING SEGMENTS of this series, 1 I have dealt with envy as an outgrowth of ideas and feelings consequent upon the infant's discovery of the need to make choices among potential relationships with his or her objects (including the self as object). When, as in infancy, greed is part of the prevailing state of mind, any realization of an actuality out of the reservior of potential choices proves to be an infuriating and outraging one—insofar as the individual is not convinced that choosing is necessary. In this paper I will develop the reason for such ideas and feelings and show that the same attitude regarding choice and choosing holds true of the choices the other makes in respect to the self. That a child is being chosen can import associative resonance from Freud's (1919) paper of a similar name.

Regarding relationships, I have particularized two fundamental states of mind—one, the COUPLE, following from and embodying the pleasure principle and involving the discovery and use of differences; the other, the PAIR, following from and embodying what I have called the selection principle and involving the need to discover or invent likeness in order to facilitate, through identifications, the formation of pairs and of groups. This is true of the relationship one takes with one's self and those relationships others seem to make with one's self. That this duality is paradigmatic means at one and the same time that choice is necessary and impossible. Accordingly, the dialectics of paradox become the lingua dicta for the study of envy.

Forewarned, the reader may now turn a cautious eye on my attempt to stick to the subject.

In my paper (1993) I questioned the soundness of trends in psychoanalysis that discount the importance of reality in psychic living or that discourage a focus upon reality on the ground that reality is difficult if not impossible to establish. Social-contructivism was referred to briefly as exemplifying the latter trend; it was not the focus of my paper.

Questions such as "Whose Reality is it Anyway?" are the offspring of these trends, as are a number of clinical stances. Among them, that the patient's subjective reality is the only reality with which we can work; that the ambiguity of our material is such that it would be arrogant for the analyst to assume that his/her grasp of the facts (or his/her capacity to accumulate data) is any more substantial than the patient's; that "there is no way" to get at what is actually going on in the analytic interaction; and that as a consequence we can interpret only on the basis of our personal perspectives.

SULLIVAN (1953) DEMANDED THAT the analyst not confuse inference with objective knowledge. He employed the phrase "bridging the gap" to highlight the analyst's mental efforts to apply meanings to the subjective experience of the patient. The analyst, he asserted, should never forget that conclusions about the subjective experience of the patient can only result in an inference, never a fact:

But when it comes to discovering what that person experienced subjectively, what meaning the situation had for him, we have only the report, the attempt to communicate by the use of words and gestures to us, of something that is extraordinarily private. … By responsive speech we are able to bridge the gap with inferences of high probability as to what is actually the case (Sullivan, 1953, p. 73).

Our panelists are taking Sullivan's challenge one step further, beyond the patient's speech and behaviors, by examining ways in which the analyst subjectively experiences the patient's "private world." The bridges of Projective Identification and Countertransference will be scrutinized to locate the nature of the links between the intrapsychic and the interpersonal within the analytic dyad. Interpersonalists are quite familiar with this task since analysis is seen in the context of an interpersonal matrix.

OUR MEDICAL COLLEAGUES WILL RECOGNIZE my title as coming from the Oath of the Aesclepiads.1 It has been in the consciousness of psychoanalysts since the inception of our profession, as evidenced in our conventional wisdom such as, "The patient leads—the analyst follows"; elegant phrases about letting ourselves become "… servant(s) of a (the patient's) process, " and, since the 1950s, our valid preoccupation with the impact of countertransference. I don't mean harm in any willful, malicious way, nor in terms of the commission of certain types of errors, those imaginative wanderings and innovations attributable to a pioneering spirit.

No, I mean harm due to our narrow, arrogant unwillingness to be puzzled or to wonder—a not wondering based on a propensity toward the sloth of certainty; or an impelling to apply learning from books, instead of our seeking out the inherent wisdom embedded in a patient's need for safety and survival, and his unspoken sensitivity to our participation, our impact. But more about that later.

This is the last issue of this Journal for which I will be responsible as senior editor.
